title: Breaking the Ice
blurb: Start a conversation with a stranger

steps.html:
Three people open a conversation with a stranger, and none of them says hello. Then four hundred floating homes on a bay in California, and the language you need to describe what the numbers are doing.

  • Hear how English opens a conversation with a stranger
  • Use the openers that make a stranger answer
  • Describe figures and proportions accurately
  • Watch a documentary about a community on the water

steps.title: Which of these would you say to a stranger?

options.label: Excuse me, is anyone sitting there?
I hope you don't mind me asking, but haven't we met somewhere before?
Sorry, but I couldn't help overhearing …
Nothing — I would wait for them to speak

steps.title: Which opener works best with a complete stranger?
options: Hello, my name is Anna. What is yours?
Excuse me, is anyone sitting there?
steps.answer: Excuse me, is anyone sitting there?
steps.why: It asks about the situation you are both in, needs only a one-word answer, and gives the other person an easy way out. Names come later, if at all.

steps.title: What do all three openers have in common?
steps.sub: Look at the pattern rather than the words.
options: They all begin with the speaker's name.
They all refer to the situation the two people are already in.
They all ask a personal question.
steps.answer: They all refer to the situation the two people are already in.
steps.why: A seat, an overheard remark, a face you half recognise. The situation does the introducing, which is why none of them needs a name.

steps.title: Turning numbers into sentences
steps.html:
Recycled from Lesson 14, aimed now at figures, charts and percentages.

To describe a proportion, English prefers a phrase to a bare number: the majority of, roughly a third of, just under half of, a significant proportion of, almost nobody, hardly any.

Be careful with the majority of: it means more than half. Forty-seven per cent is just under half, not a majority. Getting this wrong is the commonest B2 error in this area.

To describe a change, use a noun with an adjective, or a verb with an adverb: there has been a dramatic rise in … or the figure has risen dramatically. Both are correct; do not mix them into a dramatically rise.

Match the strength of your word to the size of the change: slightly → noticeably → significantly → dramatically → sharply. And note the prepositions: a rise in the number, but a rise of twelve per cent.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences built on the figures in this unit and the film.

Forty-seven per cent of Swedish homes have one resident.
The plain figure. Accurate, but flat.

Just under half of Swedish homes have one resident.
Better in prose — and not the majority.

The majority of residents still work in the city.
More than half.

There are roughly four hundred floating homes on the bay.
Roughly before a number.

A significant proportion of them were converted from old boats.
Vague but defensible.

Hardly any of the original owners are still there.
For a very small number.

There has been a dramatic rise in house prices.
Noun + adjective, and rise in.

House prices have risen dramatically.
Verb + adverb. Same meaning, other pattern.

Prices rose by twelve per cent last year.
Rise by an amount, with a verb.

That represents a rise of twelve per cent.
A rise of an amount, with a noun.

steps.title: Describing one figure three ways
steps.html:
1. The figure: 47% of homes in Sweden have a single resident, up from 32% in 1990.
  2. Say the proportion. 47% is under half, so: Just under half of Swedish homes now have a single resident. Never the majority.
  3. Say the change as a noun phrase: There has been a significant rise in the number of one-person households. Note rise in.
  4. Say the same change as a verb phrase: The proportion has risen significantly since 1990. Adverb, not adjective.
  5. Give the size, if you have it: a rise of fifteen percentage points, or the figure rose by fifteen points. Of with the noun, by with the verb.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: Why are long-time residents leaving San Francisco?
options: The city has become too quiet since the technology companies arrived.
It has the most expensive average house prices of any American city.
The shipyards that most of them worked in have finally closed.
steps.answer: It has the most expensive average house prices of any American city.
steps.why: Which is why many are moving to more affordable places just outside the city.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: How did the houseboat community begin?
options: It was built as a holiday resort in the 1960s.
People converted old boats into homes after the shipyard closed in 1945.
It was planned by the city council.
steps.answer: People converted old boats into homes after the shipyard closed in 1945.
steps.why: The area had been a huge industrial shipyard during the Second World War.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: What do residents do about the constant maintenance?
options: They employ a company to do it.
They work together, sharing knowledge, tools and labour.
They move out every few years.
steps.answer: They work together, sharing knowledge, tools and labour.
steps.why: 'The residents here work together… to ensure everybody has a safe and secure home.'

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: What has changed since the days of the hippies?

steps.title: Write a short report describing the data.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use the figures below, and describe them in words rather than repeating the numbers.
steps.placeholder: The most striking feature of the data is …
steps.html:
• Open by naming the most striking feature of the data.
  • Describe the proportions in words, not just percentages.
  • Describe one change, using either a noun + adjective or a verb + adverb.
  • Add one comparison, and say what explains it.
  • Do not call 47% a majority.

The figures

  • Homes with one resident: Sweden 47%, UK 31%, Kazakhstan 12%
  • Fastest growth in one-person households: China, India, Brazil
  • Sausalito: 400 floating homes across 5 marinas; average local house over $1m
  • Under-30s in the film's community: hardly any
  • Residents who share tools and labour: the majority
steps.modelHtml:
One-person households: what the figures show

The most striking feature of the data is the gap between countries. Just under half of Swedish homes now contain a single resident, roughly a third of British ones do, and in Kazakhstan the figure is closer to one in eight.

The fastest growth, however, is not in the countries with the highest figures. China, India and Brazil have seen the sharpest rise, largely because young adults there now move out before marriage.

The Sausalito houseboat community shows the same pressure from a different angle. Four hundred homes sit across five marinas beside a city where the average house costs over a million dollars. Hardly any of the residents are under thirty. The majority share tools and labour, which is the only reason the maintenance is manageable at all.
